div.p: Purpose Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most prevalent and lethal primary brain tumor. Non-invasive presurgical biomarkers are urgently needed to predict patients' overall survival (OS). Here we demonstrated a nuanced prognostic tool using sample entropy to assess Blood-Oxygen-Level-Dependent (BOLD) complexity and predict survival outcome, which is computationally efÏcient, reproducible, robust to noise, and readily transferable across cohorts.

Methods Resting-state fMRI from 205 treatment-naïve GBM patients and 1148 cognitively stable healthy controls were evaluated. Sample entropy (SampEn), a complexity metric, was evaluated in relation to OS at four levels: whole brain voxelwise, 15 resting state networks (RSNs), a 64-feature autoencoded latent space, and complexity dynamics along contrastenhancing (CE) boundary. Results GBM patients showed a significant reduction in global SampEn versus controls (p < 0.001). Among RSNs, medial temporal lobe (MTL) and basal ganglia (BGA) SampEn correlated inversely with OS (R² = 0.033 and 0.034; p = 0.008 and 0.006). The latent-space-dependent Cox risk score stratifies patients into high and low survival populations (p < 0.001). The number of SampEn peaks at the CE boundary also correlated negatively with OS (R² = 0.020, p = 0.037). Conclusions Voxel-wise SampEn revealed widespread loss of BOLD complexity in GBM. It identifies influences at RSNs and tumor-edge, characterizing survival. Latent space analysis revealed whole-brain SampEn characteristics, which provide a compact, data-driven biomarker that augments conventional Cox modelling and stratifies the patient survival. These findings show fMRI-derived SampEn measures are efÏcient and robust for risk stratification and mechanistic insight in glioblastoma.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most prevalent and aggressive primary brain tumor in adults, with an extremely poor prognosis [1,2]. Even with maximal resection and chemoradiotherapy, the median overall survival is approximately 14.6 months [3], and the 5-year survival rate is less than 7% [2]. GBM also has a recurrence rate of 90% [4]. Therefore, robust noninvasive presurgical biomarkers are urgently needed to stratify risk, probe mechanisms, and personalize therapy.

Studies have shown resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) can assess GBM's influence on intra-network coherence, whole-brain topology, and functional connectivity beyond the lesion, yet BOLD signal complexity has not been evaluated as a survival biomarker in GBM [5,6]. Prior rs-fMRI biomarker studies in glioma and high-grade tumors have interrogated dynamic functional connectivity states, amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF), regional homogeneity (ReHo), and graph-theoretic network properties to quantify tumor-related alterations in network organization and integration [6][7][8][9][10][11][12]. However, most rs-fMRI studies use correlations, graph metrics, or independent component analysis, which may not fully capture the dynamical changes in GBM-induced hemodynamic response [13]. Entropy metrics eliminate this limitation by quantifying the complexity of BOLD data. Specifically, sample entropy (SampEn) is parameter-light, noise-proof, and resolutioninvariant [14][15][16]. A recent study has shown SampEn in healthy brains revealed that intrinsic RSNs exhibit higher complexity than the extrinsic sensorimotor networks, and regional SampEn differentiates task from resting states [17]. These findings suggest entropy captures neurophysiological richness beyond correlation-based connectivity.

Entropy metrics also capture mechanistic insights. They quantify admissible microstate repertoire and neural configurations, including adaptive processing and flexible representation [17,18]. Entropy also reflects processing capacity as it links slower fluctuations to long-range integration and information sharing [19]. Studies have shown that higher brain signal entropy relates to better cognitive performance and adaptive behavior and has been used to characterize disease-related alterations in disorders such as Alzheimer's disease, major depression, and epilepsy [20][21][22][23][24][25][26]. These studies suggest SampEn can be both prognostic and mechanistic. As studies indicated, GBM disrupts functional connectivity in RSNs, reconfigures whole-brain topology, and interrupts neuro-vascular coupling [6,27,28]. We thus hypothesize that GBM may (i) cause loss of whole-brain complexity, (ii) disrupt network-level complexity, (iii) reveal unique tumor-core complexity dynamics, and (iv) provide accurate survival prognostic metrics.

This study applied SampEn to 205 treatment-naïve GBM patients and 1138 healthy subjects at four levels: voxel-wise whole brain topology, fifteen regions-of-interest-defined (ROIs) RSNs, whole-brain summary by latent space, and contrast-enhancing region dynamics. Overall survival was analyzed using robust linear regression, the Cox Survival Model, and Kaplan-Meier analysis. Our study suggests BOLD sample entropy analysis can serve as a nuanced, mechanistically grounded biomarker for glioblastoma prognosis.

div.head: Subjects
div.p: 205 GBM patients were recruited from patients at Washington University Medical Center neurosurgery brain tumor service between May 2012 and September 2020. Diagnosis of GBM followed appropriate WHO 2007 and 2016 guidelines and using histomorphological and immunohistochemical characteristics [29][30][31]. Characteristics include tumor cells with microvascular proliferation, pleomorphic hyperchromatic nuclei, palisading necrosis, astrocytic-like appearance, and frequent mitoses. Inclusion criteria covered a new diagnosis of brain tumor (first occurrence), biopsy or surgical treatment, and the availability of pre-surgical structural and functional MRI. Exclusion criteria included patients younger than age 18 and patients who were lost to follow-up.

Healthy subjects' data were acquired from the Midnight Scan Club (MSC) and Brain Genomics Superstruct Project (GSP). MSC includes 10 healthy, right-handed, young adults (age = 24-34 yr, 5 females and 5 males) [32]. Each subject performed 10 late-night sessions, producing 5 hours of eyes-open rs-fMRI images. GSP includes 1570 healthy, right-handed, young adults (age = 18-35 yr, 880 females and 690 males), from which we selected 1138 participants with high-quality data [33].

div.head: Clinical characteristics
div.p: Information about glioblastoma patients' demographics and the dataset are listed in Supplementary Table 1. Clinical characteristics include extent of resection (by gross total (GTR), subtotal resection (STR), and near total resection (NTR), tumor location (frontal; parietal; temporal; occipital, cingulate; other), Karnofsky Performance Status (KPS), MGMT methylation status, EGFR amplification status, TERT mutation status, and PTEN mutation status [34,35]. Overall survival was defined by the difference between the patient's first clinical visit and the date of death [36].

Comorbidities (Hx) history included stroke, seizure, deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or pulmonary embolism (PE), chronic kidney disease (CKD), diabetes, hypertension, tobacco use, hyperlipidemia, cardiac disease (myocardial infarction, arrhythmia, valvular dysfunction, and congestive heart failure), and BMI > 30. Data also recorded the presenting symptoms (Pw) including weakness, visual changes, aphasia, hydrocephalus, confusion, headache, memory impairment, and seizures.

div.head: FMRI acquisition and preprocessing
div.p: GBM patients were scanned on Siemens Trio or Skyra 3 T scanner with anatomical T1-MPRAGE, T2-FSE, FLAIR,

and eyes-open rs-fMRI. Control data was from the Midnight Scan Club and GSP with standard EPI acquisitions [32,33]. See Supplementary Material for details. The initial preprocessing involved slice-dependent time shifts compensation, systematic odd-even slice intensity differences elimination, and rigid body correction of head movement [28]. We applied voxel-wise detrending, low-pass filtering (<0.1 Hz), and nuisance regression (6 motion parameters, mean CSF), followed by 6 mm FWHM Gaussian smoothing [37,38]. Full protocol is provided in the Supplementary Material.

div.head: Tumor segmentation
div.p: Brain tumors were segmented using multimodal image acquisition, including T1w, postcontrast T1w, T2w, and FLAIR [39].

Separation of contrast-enhancing (CE) tumor, necrosis, and surrounding FLAIR hyperintense edematous areas were identified from normal cortical and subcortical tissue. In this study, a tumor is defined as CE plus the necrotic-appearing region.

div.head: Resting-state network identification
div.p: We categorized BOLD data voxels into 15 resting state networks based on a deep learning model [40,41]. Each gray matter voxel is assigned to one of the fifteen RSNs: Visual (VIS), Auditory (AUD), Somatomotor Dorsal (SMD), Somatomotor Lateral (SMI), Dorsal Attention (DAN), Ventral Attention (VAN), Salience (SAL), Frontoparietal (FPN), Cingulo-Opercular Control (CON), Default Mode (DMN), Parietal Memory (PMN), Reward (REW), Medial Temporal Lobe (MTL), Basal Ganglia (BGA), and Thalamic (THA).

div.head: Sample entropy parameters
div.p: Our study used empirically derived parameters in biological and neuroimaging data, which are embedding dimension m = 2 and tolerance r = 0.15 x SD of BOLD signal [14,15,42,43]. These two parameters balance bias and variance to generate reproducible results and reduce head-motion artifacts. Each subject underwent SampEn calculation per voxel. The illustrations of voxel-wise SampEn computation and derived metrics are shown in Supplementary Material.

div.head: Resting-state network sample entropy computation
div.p: Sample entropy for each of the 15 RSNs was calculated by averaging all the BOLD time-series voxels belonging to the network (Supplementary Fig. 1). The mean time-series was applied to the SampEn computation above. Each network SampEn was normalized by calculating the absolute difference from the average of the control population.

div.head: Autoencoder and cox model
div.p: An autoencoder compressed each patient's (n = 205) wholebrain SampEn voxels (≈65,000) to a 64-feature latent space.

The SampEn data was split into 80% train and 20% validation. The autoencoder was fit with L2 weight regularization 0.0008-0.0015, sparsity regularization 3-6, sparsity proportion 0.025-0.05, and 500-1000 epochs. The resulting 205 × 64 latent space was fit with Cox models with ridge regularization (λ ∈ {0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100}) and 5-fold CV.

The analysis included iterative LASSO-style backward elimination and bootstrap aggregation (50 resamples) with out-of-bag concordance. The Cox model quantified a risk score for each patient, which was analyzed by Kaplan-Meier analysis to stratify survival [44].

div.head: GBM tumor boundary sampen peaks
div.p: We calculated a gradient map for each GBM patient to quantify voxel-wise SampEn changes in spatial space. We then defined local maxima of the gradient map if a gradient was greater than or equal to every voxel in 3×3×3 neighborhood. The number of local maxima lying within 3 voxels of the CE boundary were defined as tumor boundary SampEn peaks, which was then correlated to OS.

div.head: Glioblastoma reduces whole brain complexity
div.p: The temporal complexity in GBM whole brain was significantly reduced compared to the healthy controls (p < 0.001; Fig. 1D). The median SampEn of healthy subjects was nearly twice that of GBM. Even contralateral SampEn, distant from the tumor, displayed a significantly lower SampEn than healthy tissue (p < 0.001; Fig. 1D). The whole-brain voxel-wise SampEn distributions of GBM patients and a healthy control are shown in Fig. 1C (Wilcoxon rank-sum p < 0.001).

We further investigated the relationship between OS and GBM CE SampEn. The results indicate that complexity loss in the tumor (region) correlates with worse OS (R 2 = 0.024, p = 0.036; Fig. 2A). We also found greater difference in whole-brain SampEn from the healthy controls correlates negatively with OS (R 2 = 0.027, p = 0.025; Fig. 2B). We then calculated the mean differences between GBM CE and contralateral regions to reduce the inter-subject variance effect. OS of GBM patients declines as the mean difference decreases (R 2 = 0.031, p = 0.016; Fig. 2C).

div.p: This study includes 205 GBM patients (age = 60.9 ± 11.4, 62.3% male) and 1148 healthy subjects (10 MSC; 1138 GSP) (Supplementary Table 1). Statistics of tumor volume, extent of resection, genetic status, Karnofsky Performance Scale (KPS), comorbidities (Hx), and presenting symptoms (Pw) are included in Supplementary Table 1. div.head: Discussion
div.p: This study demonstrates that resting-state fMRI-derived sample entropy (SampEn) provides a noninvasive prognostic biomarker in GBM. GBM caused widespread reductions in BOLD signal complexity, with greater global loss predicting shorter survival. Network-level analyses showed selective vulnerability of the medial temporal and basal ganglia networks, while heightened entropy variability at tumor margins reflected aggressive local behavior. Wholebrain autoencoder models integrating these spatial features effectively stratified patients into distinct survival groups.

Together, these results indicate that BOLD complexity captures both global network disruption and local tumor-brain interactions, offering clinically relevant insights for presurgical risk stratification and individualized management.

The observed widespread loss of BOLD complexity across the glioblastoma cohort, with healthy controls exhibiting nearly twice the median SampEn values, represents a fundamental disruption of the brain's temporal complexity architecture. This global complexity loss aligns with theoretical frameworks proposing that entropy metrics quantify the repertoire of accessible neural microstates, with higher entropy reflecting greater adaptive processing capacity and flexible information integration [17,18].

Previous studies have established that increased BOLD complexity correlates with superior cognitive performance and behavioral adaptability in healthy populations [20,22,23], suggesting that the complexity loss observed in our GBM patients reflect diminished neural variability and constrained information processing capacity. div.head: Network sample entropy characterizes GBM patient survival
div.p: Among 15 RSNs, SampEn difference in the MTL and BGA correlated negatively with OS (R² = 0.022, p = 0.042; R² = 0.038, p = 0.006 respectively; Fig. 3). Other networks did not have a significant correlation.

We evaluated MTL and BGA SampEn's effect on survival using Kasplan-Meier analysis. Patients with below-median MTL/BGA SampEn had significantly worse OS (p = 0.048* for MTL, p = 0.016* for BGA, Figs. 4A, C). An optimal split was performed to maximize the survival stratification between low and high SampEn patients (p < 0.001*** for MTL, p = 0.002** for BGA, Figs. 4B, D).

We then trained an autoencoder to produce a wholebrain-summarizing latent space, localizing SampEn's effect on GBM survival further. The performance of the final autoencoder model achieved a 59.9% explained variance and a 56.6% generalization performance (explained R 2 = 0.5951, test R 2 = 0.5663, MSE = 0.01414, Pearson correlation r = -0.004). Over 10 trials, the overfitting ratio was 1.109 ± 0.1 (moderate). The median risk score from latentspace-fitted Cox model significantly stratified GBM survival (p < 0.001***, Fig. 4E). The Cox model resulted in a hazard ratio of 3.162 with 95% CI ranging from 2.301-4.347 and p = 1.13 × 10 -12 .

The selective vulnerability of the medial temporal lobe (MTL) and basal ganglia (BGA) networks to entropy disruption, despite examining fifteen resting-state networks, reveals that glioblastoma's functional impact extends beyond simple proximity effects or anatomical burden.

The MTL network, critical for memory consolidation and episodic encoding, and the BGA network, essential for motor-cognitive integration and procedural learning, represent high-order association systems that depend on precise temporal coordination across distributed neural populations [8,9]. Their particular to complexity loss may reflect their position within the brain's hierarchical organization: both networks serve as integration hubs that synthesize information from multiple sensory and cognitive streams [8,17], making them vulnerable to the widespread connectivity disruptions induced by glioblastomas. This interpretation aligns with clinical observations that GBM patients commonly present with memory impairment, executive dysfunction, and psychomotor slowing, symptoms that map directly to MTL and BGA function, even when tumors are anatomically distant from these structures the complexity deficit extended well beyond the tumor and surrounding edema, with even contralateral brain regions showing significantly reduced SampEn compared to healthy tissue (p < 0.001; Fig. 1D). This remote effect is consistent with prior observations that glioblastomas induce widespread network reorganization and diminished functional connectivity across distributed brain systems [6,7,24]. The biological substrate for this global complexity reduction likely involves multiple mechanisms, including disrupted neurovascular coupling, altered neurotransmitter dynamics, impaired long-range connectivity, and tumor-induced metabolic stress that collectively constrain the dynamic range of neural activity patterns [3,6,27]. Although individual Sam-pEn-derived measures explain a modest fraction of survival variance (R² ≈ 0.02-0.03), this is expected given the biological and clinical heterogeneity of GBM, and their value lies in the robustness and spatial consistency of the effects across analyses. These findings suggest that glioblastomas impose a system-level constraint on brain function that transcends local structural damage, limiting the brain's capacity for neural processing. The correlation between greater numbers of boundary entropy peaks and worse survival suggests that more extensive neuron-tumor integration, reflected in widespread circuit instability at the margin, may mark more aggressive tumor behavior and enhanced invasion potential [48]. These boundary dynamics show a distinct pattern from global complexity loss. Widespread entropy reduction reflects reduced neural capacity, whereas focal increases at tumor margins suggest active tumor/neural interaction driving progression. Accordingly, the relationship between boundary SampEn peaks and survival should be interpreted as correlative rather than causal in this cohort. The combination of global suppression with local elevation highlights GBM's multi-scale functional impact and shows that entropy can capture distinct mechanisms across spatial scales. The prognostic signal in BOLD-derived sample entropy supports its potential as a noninvasive, presurgical risk-stratification tool for glioblastoma. Because it extracts prognostic information from standard resting-state fMRI, entropy metrics could be integrated with clinical workflows and used [8,9]. The negative correlation between network entropy and survival suggests that maintaining complexity in certain networks may support cognitive resilience and better outcomes. Glioblastoma's effects extend beyond tumor location, reflecting network-specific disruptions shaped by each network's computational role, connectivity, and resilience, factors that help explain individual differences in cognition and prognosis.

The identification of entropy peaks at the contrastenhancing tumor boundary, with their negative correlation to survival, provides novel insight into the pathophysiological dynamics at the tumor-brain interface. Unlike the global reduction observed throughout the brain, these localized entropy elevations represent spatial heterogeneity in BOLD signal patterns that likely reflects the unique biological processes occurring at the tumor margin. Recent discoveries of neuron-glioma synaptic integration and peritumoral hyperexcitability offer compelling mechanistic explanations for these entropy spikes [45][46][47]. Glioma cells form functional synapses with neurons and become electrically integrated into existing neural circuits, creating zones of aberrant excitability and dysregulated neural activity at the tumor periphery [46,47]. div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Sample entropy derived from resting-state fMRI represents a robust prognostic biomarker for glioblastoma and an applicable framework for quantifying neural complexity. BOLD complexity loss correlates with overall survival across multiple spatial scales, from whole-brain patterns and tumor boundaries to specific disruptions in medial temporal lobe and basal ganglia networks, suggesting a methodological advance in entropy mapping to networklevel pathophysiology. By quantifying temporal complexity dynamics, sample entropy provides both prognostic stratification and mechanistic insight into glioblastoma's disruption of brain function, highlighting theoretical connections between neural variability, network integration, and tumor-brain interactions. These findings support entropy-based measures as potentially useful adjuncts to traditional neuroimaging for presurgical risk assessment and personalized treatment planning and motivate future studies integrating SampEn with clinical and molecular markers in multi-site cohorts. alongside anatomical and molecular biomarkers to improve patient selection and treatment planning. Local peritumoral entropy peaks may also help guide surgical and radiation strategies. Thus, sample-entropy measures are practical for multi-site use and for combining with other data to refine individualized neuro-oncologic decision-making.

div.head: Limitations
div.p: This study has several limitations. The GBM cohort came from a single center. Future studies will involve validation on outside cohorts to assess generalizability. We also cannot fully exclude residual motion-related artifacts or infer causal trajectories from this cross-sectional design. Our network-level RSN entropy used voxel averages, which can mask spatial heterogeneity, and tumor-boundary entropy depended on chosen gradient/threshold parameters that could alter local patterns. The autoencoder was trained with a fixed split and architecture, so broader hyperparameter tuning, cross-validation, and multi-site validation are needed to confirm robustness. (green).
